title: What Citizenship Is
hook: Citizenship is the formal bond between a person and a state — the status that turns a resident into a full member, with rights and duties to match.
key_points: Citizenship is legal membership in a state, carrying rights and obligations.
It is usually acquired by birth (by place or by descent) or by naturalization.
Rights often include voting, protection, and a passport; duties may include obeying law, taxes, jury or military service.
It differs from mere residency, which lacks the full political membership citizenship confers.
content_html: Citizenship is the formal legal relationship between an individual and a state — the status that makes someone a full member of a political community rather than simply a person who happens to live there. That membership is a two-way bond. On one side it grants rights: typically the right to vote and stand for office, the protection of the state at home and abroad, an unconditional right to enter and remain, and a passport. On the other side it carries duties, which vary by country but often include obeying the law, paying taxes, and sometimes serving on juries or in the armed forces.
extra_html: People usually become citizens in one of two ways. Citizenship by birth is granted either by place of birth (being born on a country's territory) or by descent (being born to citizen parents) — countries weight these differently. Citizenship can also be acquired later through naturalization, the legal process by which a long-term resident meets certain requirements and is formally admitted as a citizen. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the precise bundle of rights and duties attached to citizenship differs across states and has expanded over history. The key distinction to hold onto is between citizenship and residency: many people live lawfully in a country as residents, working and paying taxes, without being citizens — and it is citizenship, not residency, that confers the full political membership at the heart of self-government, above all the right to help choose who governs.

related.title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
related.hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

related.title: Civil Liberties vs Civil Rights
related.hook: Two terms people mix up: liberties are freedoms from government interference; rights are protections to be treated equally.

related.title: Ways to Participate
related.hook: Voting is the headline act of citizenship — but it's only one of many ways people shape politics, from joining a party to signing a petition or marching.

related.title: How Parades and Festivals Redefine 'One of Us'
related.hook: A Lunar New Year 5K, a Fourth of July parade with a woman in a sari, a festival that reclaims a slur — public celebrations quietly redraw who counts as a full member of the community.

flashcards.back_html: Legal membership in a state — a formal bond carrying rights (like voting and protection) and obligations (like obeying the law).

flashcards.prompt: What are the two most common ways people acquire citizenship?

choices.text: By birth (place or descent) or by naturalization
By winning an election or buying a passport
Only by serving in the military

flashcards.explanation_html: Most people are citizens by birth — by where they were born or who their parents are — or become citizens later through naturalization.

flashcards.prompt: How does citizenship differ from simply residing in a country?

choices.text: Citizenship confers full political membership; residency alone does not
There is no difference at all
Residents have more rights than citizens

flashcards.explanation_html: Residents may live and work in a state, but citizenship adds the full political membership — typically including the right to vote.
